title: The Talking Parrot
summary: Akbar decrees that whoever brings news of his favorite parrot's death shall be executed. When the bird dies, Birbal delivers the news without speaking the fatal words.
full_text:
A foreign ambassador presented Emperor Akbar with a rare green parrot from the forests of Ceylon. The bird was extraordinary: its emerald plumage shone like jade, and it could recite Persian couplets, greet the Emperor by name, and sing melodious hymns. Akbar loved the bird dearly, housing it in a golden cage in the royal bedchamber.

Fearing for the bird's safety, Akbar issued a rash and terrible imperial decree:

'This parrot is my favorite companion. I command the royal caretakers to guard it with their lives. And hear this well: whoever brings me the news that my beloved parrot is dead shall be executed on the spot!'

A year passed. One morning, the chief bird caretaker walked into the bedchamber and found the parrot lying stiff on the bottom of the cage, its eyes closed, its claws cold in death.

The poor caretaker was paralyzed with terror. 'If I tell the Emperor the parrot is dead, I will be executed! If I hide it, I will be executed as a traitor!' Weeping uncontrollably, the man ran to Birbal's house.

Birbal listened to the plight, patted the caretaker's shoulder, and said: 'Do not fear, my friend. Go home to your family; I shall inform the Emperor myself.'

Birbal walked into the Diwan-i-Khas, where Akbar was holding court. Birbal approached the throne with folded hands and a serene expression:

'Your Majesty, I have just visited your royal parrot.'

Akbar smiled: 'How is my magnificent bird today? Is it singing?'

Birbal replied with quiet gravity: 'Sire, your parrot is in a state of profound contemplation. It lies peacefully on its back at the bottom of the golden cage. Its eyes are closed; its beak does not open; its wings do not flutter; it breathes no air, eats no seeds, and drinks no water.'

Akbar frowned, leaning forward: 'Why does it not move or breathe? Is it dead?'

Birbal bowed low, his eyes twinkling with profound respect:

'Your Majesty has spoken the word, not I! The Emperor himself has announced the news!'

Akbar gasped, then paused. The realization of his own foolish decree hit him. If anyone had spoken the words 'the parrot is dead,' Akbar's cruel decree would have demanded an innocent man's blood. But Birbal's tactful description had led the Emperor to utter the truth himself, rendering the death decree powerless!

Akbar smiled with deep relief and gratitude:

'Birbal, your tact has saved an innocent life and preserved your Emperor from committing a grave sin of tyranny.' Akbar rewarded Birbal and abolished the foolish decree forever.

quiz.question: What is the central moral lesson taught in "The Talking Parrot"?
options: Acting in haste and anger without thinking
Believing rumors and flattery without proof
